title: Character classification and conversion with ctype.h
learningObjectives: Explain the language rule and its constraints.
Trace the example and predict its output.
Identify relevant boundary and safety cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: ctype.h provides functions such as isalpha, isdigit, isspace, tolower and toupper. Their argument must be EOF or a value representable as unsigned char.
understand.whyItMatters: This concept supports correct handling of C data and helps prevent invalid memory access or incorrect program behaviour.
understand.analogy: Think of the construct as a precisely bounded sequence of storage and operations.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's rules for object lifetime, bounds, types or undefined behaviour.

explain.narrative:
ctype.h provides functions such as isalpha, isdigit, isspace, tolower and toupper. Their argument must be EOF or a value representable as unsigned char.

Always check the types, object bounds and preconditions required by the operation. Compile with warnings enabled and test ordinary as well as boundary inputs.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.code: Plain char may be signed. Passing a negative char value directly to a ctype function can cause undefined behaviour; convert through unsigned char first.

practise.guidedTask: Each byte is converted to unsigned char before classification. Letters are printed in uppercase; the space and digits remain unchanged.
practise.independentTask: Predict the output and count the alphabetic characters.
hints: Count digits and whitespace in a string, using a valid ctype argument.
ctype functions follow the active C locale and are not a complete Unicode text-processing system.
Do not assume isdigit returns exactly one; use it as a truth value.
